memoria-unificada.d: An architecture in which the CPU and GPU use the same physical RAM pool, as in the GB10 (DGX Spark, 128 GB of LPDDR5X) and Apple M chips. There's no copy over PCIe, but the OS, page cache, processes, weights and KV compete for the same capacity and the same bandwidth.

page-cache.d: Copies of chunks of files that Linux keeps in RAM after reading or writing them. Clean pages can be dropped at any moment. On the GB10's UMA they count as memory “used” by the GPU.

memfree.d: The /proc/meminfo field with the pages that have no owner at all. On the GB10, torch.cuda.mem_get_info() returns this number, which is why page cache appears to “occupy” the GPU.

memavailable.d: The kernel's estimate of how much can be allocated without resorting to swap: MemFree minus the reserves, plus the page cache and reclaimable slab (each with the low-mark discount). It's the number vLLM's boot check uses on an integrated GPU, and the one the recipes watch.

memoria-anonima.d: Process memory with no file behind it (heap, stack, CPU tensors). It can't be dropped: the only way out of RAM is to swap.

drop-caches.d: echo 1 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches drops the clean page cache of the whole system; echo 3 also drops dentries and inodes. It requires root and doesn't work inside a container without CAP_SYS_ADMIN.

posix-fadvise.d: A call that tells the kernel a file's pages won't be used anymore. For clean pages, the kernel drops them. It works without root and only on the files you open, as Qwen's evict_page_cache.py does.

tamanho-de-pagina.d: The kernel's unit of memory management: 4 KiB on x86 and on most ARM kernels; the GLM kit runs a custom kernel (6.17.13-rocket64k) with 64 KiB pages. On that kernel, H2D copies from file-backed mmap hung the driver. Check with getconf PAGESIZE.

o-direct.d: An open() flag that makes the disk transfer data straight into a process buffer, bypassing the page cache. It requires aligned buffers and sizes. It's what InstantTensor uses.

h2d.d: A host → device copy (cudaMemcpyAsync/cuMemcpyHtoDAsync). On UMA it doesn't cross PCIe, but it still goes through the driver and the DMA engine, which need stable sources.

instanttensor.d: A safetensors loader with direct I/O (O_DIRECT) and a ring of pinned buffers with many reads in flight. In GLM it loads 164 GiB in ~36–70 s, versus ~290–300 s for the default loader, but leaves ~4–5 GiB less KV.

read-ahead.d: Reading ahead what will probably be requested next (the next shard) to hide disk latency. It increases page cache occupancy while it lasts.

gpu-memory-utilization.d: The fraction of the device's total memory that vLLM may budget for weights, activations, non-torch allocations and KV; CUDA graphs are included only if VLLM_MEMORY_PROFILER_ESTIMATE_CUDAGRAPHS=1. On the GB10's UMA, each 0.01 ≈ 1.2 GiB taken from the operating system. The recipes use 0.75–0.87.

profile-run.d: vLLM's test pass at boot, with the largest single-step batch, to measure peak activations (and, with VLLM_MEMORY_PROFILER_ESTIMATE_CUDAGRAPHS=1, estimate the CUDA graphs). The KV gets whatever is left of the budget. --kv-cache-memory-bytes pins the KV and skips that derivation.

caching-allocator.d: The PyTorch layer that asks the driver for large segments and slices them into blocks. Freed blocks stay in the cache (reserved, not allocated) for fast reuse. Configured via PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF.

fragmentacao.d: Free memory scattered across holes that can't serve a large request. In the PyTorch allocator, holes in different segments don't merge, and reserved memory grows beyond allocated memory. expandable_segments:True reduces the problem.

expandable-segments.d: A PyTorch allocator option that uses one segment per stream, which grows by mapping physical pages into a contiguous virtual range. It reduces fragmentation, but some vLLM KV connectors reject it.

swap.d: A disk area where the kernel sends anonymous pages when RAM runs short, bringing them back the next time they're touched. On the GB10, paging out vLLM memory can hang the UVM driver.

swappiness.d: A parameter (0–200) that says how much the kernel prefers sending anonymous memory to swap over dropping page cache. With 0, swap isn't forbidden, just postponed until pressure gets severe. The Spark ships with 0; GLM pins it, and the package measured while exploring Qwen's TP1 used 30.

uvm.d: The NVIDIA driver subsystem (nvidia-uvm) that manages pages accessible by both CPU and GPU. On the GB10, GPU allocations go through it, and it shows up in cgroup OOM logs.

livelock.d: A state in which a system is active but makes no progress. On the GB10, the UVM driver spins: GPU at ~96% drawing 12–20 W, token counters frozen and /health still returning 200.

watermarks.d: Per-zone min/low/high thresholds of free memory. Below low, kswapd reclaims in the background; below min, whoever is allocating reclaims on its own. They're computed from vm.min_free_kbytes and vm.watermark_scale_factor.

kswapd.d: The kernel thread that reclaims memory in the background (drops page cache, sends pages to swap) when free memory falls below the low mark, until it gets back to the high mark.

cgroup.d: The Linux mechanism that limits and accounts for the memory of a group of processes (docker --memory, memory.max, memory.current). On the GB10, Qwen's own HANDOFF disagrees with itself on how much of the GPU allocations is counted.

watchdog-memoria.d: A process that periodically reads available memory and kills the service before disaster strikes, like memwatch.sh (1 s, 6 GiB floor). On its own, it can't catch collapses of GiB per second.

earlyoom.d: A userspace daemon that kills processes when available memory gets low. DeepSeek turns it off because, under deep context, it can kill vLLM.

nv-err-no-memory.d: An NVIDIA driver error (visible in journalctl -k) raised when an internal allocation fails. On the GB10 it's the early signal that the unified pool has hit the ceiling.

offload.d: Moving tensors or computation from the GPU to the CPU. On a discrete GPU, it frees VRAM. On UMA it doesn't free physical memory, but it can reduce UVM pressure and, with mmap, make pages evictable.

meta-device.d: PyTorch's “make-believe” device: tensors with a shape and dtype but no memory. It lets you build an entire model for free and materialize only the parts you need.

cuda-ipc.d: Sharing a GPU allocation between processes through a handle (cudaIpcGetMemHandle/OpenMemHandle). The PLE offload writes into each rank's GPU buffer this way.

zmq.d: A socket-based message queue library (PUSH/PULL, PUB/SUB patterns). vLLM uses it between processes, with msgpack to serialize the requests.

stream-memory-ops.d: cuStreamWaitValue32/cuStreamWriteValue32: the GPU stream waits for or writes an integer in memory, and this can be captured in a CUDA graph. The GB10 reports CAN_USE_STREAM_MEM_OPS = 0.

cuda-graph.d: A sequence of kernels recorded once and replayed without the CPU launch cost. It only works for the captured shapes, and operations that depend on the host aren't re-executed inside it.

nconnect.d: An NFS mount option that opens N TCP connections to the server and spreads the requests among them. With nconnect=8, a cold load can fill the 200 Gb/s cable.

reserva-do-host.d: Memory that TensorFold's startup keeps out of the budget: the budget is the MemAvailable at startup minus the reserve. The default is max(4 GiB, a tenth of RAM); TENSORFOLD_MEMORY_RESERVE_GIB replaces it (the TensorFold variant of the GLM recipe uses 14.5). It also carries what the estimate doesn't count (CUDA context, NCCL, workspaces) and, because of that, sets the lowest free memory at the peak.

estimativa-de-partida.d: The math TensorFold does before allocating: weights read only from the safetensors headers, a staging peak for loading and the caches from a bytes-per-token formula. A binary search finds the largest window that fits the budget; if the requested one doesn't fit, startup refuses without loading anything. It replaces vLLM's profile run.

paginas-estacionadas.d: Free pages the kernel (6.7+) leaves on its per-CPU lists (pagesets in /proc/zoneinfo) after a bulk free: they count in neither MemFree nor MemAvailable and come back slowly. In the GLM·TF recipe, 5–9 GiB after the image copy; patch 0122 counts them in the startup budget.

reserva-de-tela.d: The ~2 GiB the GB10 firmware sets aside for a monitor, outside MemAvailable. On a headless Spark they sit idle; the GLM·TF recipe can lend them to the KV pool (DISPLAY_KV_MIB, patches 0072 and 0087).
